newsitem.title: USA: Lake, CIA choice, tries to wed power and principle.
newsitem.headline: Lake, CIA choice, tries to wed power and principle.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice as director of central intelligence, Anthony Lake, is a soft-spoken, self-mocking intellectual who has spent his career trying to reconcile U.S. power and principle.
As the president's national security adviser, Lake, 57, has been the point man of Clinton's foreign policy ups and downs since the president took office in January 1993.

He earned a reputation for sticking to his principles when he quit the staff of President Richard Nixon's national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, in protest at the secret bombing of Cambodia in 1970. Lake argued the bombing would destroy Cambodia and rekindle violence at home prompted by protests to the Indochina War.

In accepting the nomination on Thursday to become the top U.S. spymaster, Lake said he was "to put it mildly, very enthusiastic" about the job. He will head the Central Intelligence Agency and serve as board chairman of its 12 companion spy outfits in the executive branch.

"I firmly believe that in the post-Cold War world, the role of the CIA is more important than ever in defending Americans against the threats of terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, in explaining clearly the activities of governments in an ever-more complicated world and in giving the president the unvarnished facts on which he can base wise decisions in a time of change and promise," he said.

Lake, who says he dreads the limelight, generally prefers to assume the cloak of an unnamed senior official, speaking to reporters on background. Self-mockingly, he called his old job "national security adviser of the free world."
He has been known to quote from the children's book and film character Winnie the Pooh.

Anthony Lake is a Yankee aristocrat who joined the State Department in 1962. He was one of a handful of bright young liberals hired by Kissinger, then President Nixon's national security adviser, to help extricate the United States from the Vietnam quagmire.
Lake later wrote a book highly criticial of Kissinger's approach to policy on Africa during the Nixon presidency.
The 1976 book, the "Tar Baby Option," criticised the policy of easing U.S. opposition to white minority rule in South Africa while appeasing black African governments with foreign aid and kind words.
He is also the author of the 1989 book about Nicaragua, "Somoza Falling", and a co-author of the 1984 "Our Own Worst Enemy: The Unmaking of American Foreign Policy."

Like Clinton, Lake studied in Britain after receiving his undergraduate degree. He spent two years studying international economics at Cambridge University's Trinity College after graduating from Harvard College. He holds a doctoral degree from Princeton University's Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs.

Lake helped start the quarterly journal Foreign Policy with fellow State Department veterans John Campbell and Richard Holbrooke. The journal is an alternative to the more establishment quarterly, Foreign Affairs.

Prior to joining the Clinton administration, he divided his time between his farm in western Massachusetts and Mount Holyoke College, where he had been a professor of international relations since 1981.
Lake was born on April 2, 1939, in New York City. He and his wife Antonia Plehn Lake have three children, Timothy, Eleanor and Eliza.
